strengths: Introduces a part-level spatial representation, the Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG), with two-level object/part nodes and part-level geometric edges that encode fine-grained relations such as on, in, against, and aligned with specific surfaces. This addresses a real limitation of object-level scene graphs and linguistic prepositions for spatial reasoning and physically grounded generation.

Proposes a Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver that instantiates PAGs via coarse localization, part-level alignment, and final pose sampling/validation, then applies physics simulation. The approach is conceptually sound and supports collision-free, physically plausible scene synthesis.

Constructs PARSE-10K, a large-scale dataset of 10,000 indoor 3D scenes with part-segmented assets, part-level contact annotations, physical optimization, and real-image-guided layout priors. The dataset fills an important gap: existing datasets generally lack dense part-level contact supervision and physical optimization.

Provides empirical evidence that fine-tuning a VLM (Qwen3-VL) on PARSE-10K improves spatial reasoning, with reported gains over GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robobrain2.0, and zero-shot Qwen3-VL on visual relation MCQ, part-level contact MCQ, and scene graph generation tasks.

Includes a scene-generation study showing that PARSE-10K-trained models conditioned on PAGs produce scenes with higher user-rated complexity, realism, and contact fidelity than InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT and than an unconditioned variant.
The paper is generally well motivated, clearly written, and includes helpful illustrative figures that explain the PAG hierarchy and solver pipeline.
weaknesses: The core technical method is described mostly at a high level. There are no formal definitions, equations, algorithms, or optimization details for the Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver; constraint representation, topological traversal, and part-level geometric reasoning are left to the supplementary. This limits technical depth and reproducibility.

The spatial reasoning evaluation only fine-tunes Qwen3-VL and compares it to mostly zero-shot general VLMs. It does not compare against models fine-tuned on prior datasets (e.g., 3D-FRONT) or ablate PAG components. Thus the reported gains may reflect fine-tuning on the dataset rather than the part-level representation specifically.

The MCQ tasks are generated from the same synthetic rendered scene distribution used for training, and the manually labeled real-image COCO evaluation set is not reported separately. This makes generalization to real-world spatial reasoning unclear.

Scene generation evaluation relies primarily on qualitative examples and a small user study (20 participants, 12 rendered scenes) without standard quantitative metrics, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The comparison is also limited mainly to InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT.

Table 1 is ambiguous/inconsistent in reporting dataset statistics. For PARSE-10K, the '# Objects' column (17,372 assets) conflicts with 'Avg.Objects' (49.9 objects per scene), and similar inconsistencies appear for other datasets, making dataset scale comparisons difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility is not fully demonstrated: the paper does not specify code release, model weights, or complete training/solver hyperparameters in the main text, and the solver depends on multiple external components (Sapien, Michelangelo, CLIP) that are not fully detailed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: object-level scene graphs and linguistic prepositions (on, in, against) are too coarse to disambiguate which parts actually support or contact one another, and the authors make a convincing case that part-level relations are the right granularity for physically grounded spatial modeling.

The Part-Centric Assembly Graph (PAG) is a clean, well-formalized representation: a two-level node hierarchy (object nodes as semantic queries, part nodes with labeled surfaces) and two-granularity edges (object-level and part-level geometric edges), with the DAG property making constraint solving tractable and physically realizable.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is technically sound and well-motivated: a coarse-to-fine refinement (coarse localization → part-level alignment → final pose sampling and validation) that progressively shrinks the feasible pose space, plus SAPIEN physics simulation for plausibility. Figure 3 nicely illustrates the coarse-to-fine controllability and the effect of different part-level relations.

The PARSE-10K dataset is a substantial and useful contribution: 10,000 scenes, ~17,372 part-segmented assets, 132 categories, ~49.9 objects/scene, with part-level contact annotations and contact graphs. Table 1 makes the gap versus prior datasets (HSSD, 3D-FRONT, FurniScene, etc.) explicit and convincing.

The evaluation spans multiple complementary tasks — visual-relation MCQ, part-level contact MCQ, scene graph generation, and 3D scene generation with a user study — and the fine-tuned model shows clear gains over strong baselines (e.g., 97.4 vs. 86.2 on visual relation, 86.2 vs. 60.4 on part-level contact, and large SGG improvements). The grounding-agnostic SGG metric is a thoughtful addition to disentangle grounding from relational reasoning.

The manuscript is generally clear, well-organized, and the figures (overview, PAG example, solver pipeline, dataset gallery) aid comprehension. Limitations (canonical-pose sensitivity, difficulty with highly oblique contacts, manual PAG construction) are acknowledged.
The inclusion of real COCO images in the MCQ test set is a good step toward demonstrating some generalization beyond the synthetic distribution.
weaknesses: The central VLM comparison is potentially unfair or at least conflates two effects: a Qwen3-VL model fine-tuned on the proposed data is compared against generalist, off-the-shelf GPT-5 / Gemini-2.5-Pro / Claude-Opus-4. A fine-tuned model trained on the evaluation distribution is expected to win, so the reported margins do not by themselves demonstrate that the part-level representation is superior. Comparisons against fine-tuned variants of other models (or against other part-aware / spatially grounded methods) would be needed to isolate the contribution of the representation.

The evaluation tasks (visual-relation MCQ, part-level contact MCQ, and the scene-graph targets) are constructed from the same synthetic dataset used for training, and the train/test split is not described. This raises concerns about distribution overlap and possible leakage; it is unclear how much of the reported improvement reflects genuine relational understanding versus in-distribution fitting.

Scene generation is evaluated primarily qualitatively (Figure 6) plus a small user study (20 participants, 12 scenes, Table 3). There are no quantitative metrics for the generated scenes — e.g., collision-free rate, physical-stability scores, part-level contact fidelity, or distributional metrics — making the generation claims ("substantially improved physical realism and structural complexity") only weakly supported. Notably, Ours(uncond) is worse than InstructScene on realism (27.5% vs. 33.8%), so the benefit appears contingent on PAG conditioning, which deserves more rigorous quantification.

The dataset is generated by the same PARSE solver that is later used to produce supervision/targets, creating a potential self-consistency loop: models trained on PARSE-10K may learn the solver's artifacts and canonical-pose conventions rather than genuine physical relationships, which could inflate downstream results and limit transfer.

There is no component ablation isolating the value of the part-level edges versus object-level edges, or the contribution of individual solver stages (coarse localization, part-level alignment, physics refinement). Without such ablations, the specific design choices that drive the gains remain unclear.

Scalability and generalization of PAG construction are uncertain: as acknowledged, relations require part-specific coordinate reasoning and partially manual construction, and the directional-face contact model may fail on highly oblique or multi-contact configurations. How this scales to arbitrary objects or open-vocabulary categories is not demonstrated.

Dataset/code/model availability and the details needed for reproducibility (train/test splits, annotation protocols, number of manually curated relations) are not clearly stated in the main text, which weakens the reproducibility of both the dataset and the reported numbers.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine limitation of object-level scene graphs: linguistic prepositions (on, in, against) are too coarse to specify which surfaces actually contact or support one another, and a part-level formulation is a reasonable way to address this ambiguity.

The Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) is a clean, well-described representation: a two-level node structure (object nodes as semantic queries, part nodes with labeled canonical surfaces) plus coarse object-level edges and fine-grained part-level geometric edges, organized as a DAG to make assembly tractable.

PARSE-10K is a potentially useful resource. Table 1 shows it is larger than several existing indoor datasets and is unique in simultaneously providing part annotations, part-level contact annotations, and physical optimization; the scale (10K scenes, 17,372 part-segmented assets, 132 categories) is substantial.

The demonstration of fine-grained relational control (Fig. 3c) is a nice illustration: changing a part-level relation (e.g., Book cover-bottom 'On' vs 'Leaning Against' shelf) yields distinct, predictable arrangements, which is the kind of controllability that object-level systems cannot offer.

The paper makes a breadth-wise effort across multiple downstream tasks (spatial MCQ, part-level contact MCQ, scene graph generation, scene generation) and includes a user study, which shows the dataset is intended to be reusable beyond a single benchmark.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is confounded. 'Ours' is Qwen3-VL fine-tuned on PARSE-10K and evaluated on test sets derived from PARSE-10K, while every baseline (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robobrain2.0, Qwen3-VL) is zero-shot. No control is provided that fine-tunes a baseline on an alternative in-domain dataset (e.g., 3D-FRONT-derived annotations) at equal scale, so the reported gains on Visual Relation (97.4 vs 86.2) and SGG (76.6 F1 vs 44.2) cannot be attributed to part-level supervision or to the framework.

No ablation separates part-level supervision from object-level supervision, even though 'a part-level formulation is needed' is the paper's central thesis. Without this, the key claim remains unverified.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is the core technical contribution yet is never quantitatively evaluated: there is no runtime, success-rate, or comparison against rejection sampling or prior constraint solvers. Assertions such as 'sharply reducing the feasible space,' 'far more efficient generation,' and poses being 'guaranteed a priori' to satisfy constraints are stated without supporting measurements.

Scene generation is evaluated only qualitatively plus a small user study (20 participants, 12 scenes). No quantitative metrics are reported (collision/penetration rates, physical stability after simulation, relation accuracy of generated scenes, distributional metrics). Critically, Table 3 shows 'Ours(uncond)' is rated less realistic than InstructScene (27.5% vs 33.8%), which undercuts the claim that PARSE-10K itself improves scene generation; the gains depend entirely on PAG conditioning, not the dataset alone.

The spatial-reasoning MCQs are constructed from the same PARSE-10K distribution the model is fine-tuned on, and distractors are generated by 'randomly replacing object and relation labels.' This is essentially an in-distribution label-detection task, so the 97.4% accuracy is not strong evidence of spatial reasoning; no human baseline or upper bound is reported.
The paper mentions adding manually labeled real COCO images to the test set to check generalization, but no separate real-image results are reported, so the generalization claim is unsubstantiated.

The dataset construction pipeline is under-specified. It is not explained how PAGs are extracted from real images, how the 'real-image layout priors' are obtained, or how the asset retrieval is performed, which hinders reproducibility. The 'compositional diversity' claim is also questionable: ~10,000 scenes at ~49.9 objects each (~500K instances) drawn from only 17,372 unique assets implies roughly 29 reuses per asset.

Physical plausibility of PARSE-10K is asserted ('dense contact structures,' 'physically valid') but never quantified for the released dataset (e.g., stability or interpenetration statistics after simulation), so the property used to justify the dataset is not measured.

Several conclusions are overstated relative to the evidence ('substantially improved physical realism and structural complexity,' 'significantly advances geometry-grounded spatial reasoning'), and Table 2's 'With BBox Matching / No BBox Matching' presentation makes it hard to disentangle grounding from relational reasoning.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated part-level formulation of spatial relations, correctly identifying that linguistic prepositions ('on', 'in', 'against') are underspecified regarding which regions actually support, contain, or contact one another; the 'book on a table' example (spine vs. cover) is a crisp illustration of a real limitation of existing object-level scene graphs.

The Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) is a technically sound representation: a hierarchical DAG with object nodes (semantic queries) and part nodes (with labeled surfaces), plus two granularities of edges (object-level spatial edges for coarse layout, part-level geometric edges for fine-grained control). The assembly-centric DAG view for sequential, collision-aware instantiation is a sensible design.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is elegantly structured as a coarse-to-fine procedure (coarse localization, part-level alignment, final sampling/validation), and the deterministic accumulation of constraints reduces blind rejection sampling—a reasonable engineering choice.

PARSE-10K is a substantial artifact: 10,000 scenes, 17,372 part-segmented assets, 132 categories, average 49.9 objects per scene, and a part-level contact graph. Table 1 usefully situates it against HSSD-200, 3D-FRONT, FumiScene, and METASCENES along layout method, physics optimization, and part-level annotation axes.

The VLM results are strong and internally consistent (97.4% visual relation MCQ, 86.2% part-level contact MCQ, large lead on Scene Graph Generation), and the paper adds a grounding-agnostic metric to separate relational reasoning from bounding-box localization quality, which is a thoughtful evaluation refinement.

The paper is clearly written and the supplement is thorough, including Algorithm 1, a comprehensive spatial-relation dictionary (Table 4), asset-library construction, and implementation details that aid reproducibility.
The qualitative scene-generation comparisons (Fig. 6) and the conditional-vs-unconditional user study are informative about how PAG conditioning affects generation.
weaknesses: The VLM evaluation is fundamentally confounded. The 'Ours' model is Qwen3-VL fine-tuned on PARSE-10K with task-format-specific supervision (multi-task MCQ + SGG), yet it is compared against zero-shot general VLMs (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robobrain2.0) that have never seen this task format. The central claim—that part-level supervision yields better spatial reasoning—is therefore not isolated. A baseline fine-tuned on object-level data (e.g., 3D-FRONT) with the same task format is missing and is necessary to attribute the gains to the part-level annotations rather than to fine-tuning.

The scene-generation evidence is weak. The paper reports no standard quantitative metrics (FID, KID, etc.) and relies on a small user study (20 participants, 12 scenes) whose scene-selection protocol is not described. More importantly, Table 3 shows the unconditional PARSE-10K model performs worse than InstructScene (3D-FRONT) on realism (27.5% vs 33.8%) and contact fidelity (26.3% vs 28.8%), and the paper's own analysis attributes the conditional model's success to PAG control rather than to the dataset. This undercuts the claim that PARSE-10K alone 'facilitates the generation of more complex and realistic scenes.'

Dataset diversity is overstated. Section C.2 states that 10,000 scenes are produced from only 200 distinct PAG templates (about 50 scenes per template). Calling these '10,000 unique indoor scenes' overstates diversity, and the comparison to FumiScene (111k scenes) and 3D-FRONT (18.9k scenes) in Table 1 ignores the template-limited variability of the generated scenes.

Physical validity—one of the paper's central selling points—is not quantitatively reported. The solver's success/failure rate, the proportion of scenes surviving Sapien stabilization, and the post-simulation stability are not given, despite 'physically consistent 3D scenes' being a headline claim.

The 'part-level contact annotations' are computed from simulation (proximity ≤1mm on COACD convex hulls) rather than human-verified ground truth. Presenting these as 'annotations' (Table 1 column 'Part-Level Contact Annots.') overstates their provenance; they are derived labels, and their fidelity to real contact semantics is not evaluated.

PAG construction is acknowledged in the conclusion to be 'partially manual and sensitive to canonical poses,' which materially limits the scalability and applicability of the proposed pipeline. The manual verification of canonical poses for 132 categories is also a significant hidden cost.

Ablations on the PAG components are missing. It is unclear how much of the benefit comes from object-level edges vs. part-level geometric edges, from the specific relation dictionary, or from the DAG topological ordering. Similarly, no experiment isolates the contribution of the fine-tuning data vs. the task format.

Some baseline comparisons are not informative for the tasks evaluated (e.g., SGG with GPT-5, which was not designed for structured graph output with bounding boxes); the resulting gap is expected and does not by itself demonstrate dataset value.

The claim that the model generalizes to real images is supported only by a single qualitative example (Fig. 1a). No quantitative results on the added COCO real-image subset are reported, so synthetic-to-real transfer is asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated part-centric representation (PAG) that explicitly models object-level spatial edges and part-level geometric edges, addressing the ambiguity of object-level scene graphs and linguistic prepositions such as on/in/against.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is technically detailed: it converts PAG relations into geometric constraints, progressively reduces the feasible pose space, validates collisions, and applies physical simulation. The relation dictionary and Algorithm 1 in the supplement support reproducibility.

Constructs PARSE-10K, a large-scale dataset of 10,000 indoor scenes with 17,372 part-segmented assets across 132 categories and dense part-level contact annotations. Table 1 shows it fills a clear gap relative to HSSD-200, 3D-FRONT, FurniScene, and METASCENES in part annotations and physical optimization.

Provides strong empirical support for spatial reasoning: fine-tuned Qwen3-VL reaches 97.4% visual relation MCQ, 86.2% part-level contact MCQ, and 76.6/78.2 SGG F1, outperforming GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robotbrain2.0, and zero-shot Qwen3-VL by substantial margins.

Demonstrates downstream usefulness for 3D scene generation: PAG-conditioned diffusion produces more complex, realistic, and contact-faithful scenes in qualitative comparisons and a user study, with clear gains over InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT.

The paper is generally clear and well illustrated. Figures 2 and 3 effectively explain the PAG structure and the coarse-to-fine solver, while the supplement gives substantial implementation details, training hyperparameters, prompt templates, and asset-construction procedures.

Acknowledges key limitations honestly, including the complexity of relation definitions, dependence on canonical poses, and manual aspects of PAG construction, which helps frame the contribution and future work.
weaknesses: The PAG relation vocabulary and construction pipeline remain partially manual and dependent on curated canonical-pose assets. The 200 base PAGs are manually designed and then scaled to 10,000 scenes, which may limit compositional diversity and generalization to uncurated real-world layouts.

The solver is not directly evaluated with metrics such as constraint-satisfaction rate, collision-free success rate, failure rate, or runtime. Its effectiveness is inferred mainly from downstream VLM and scene-generation results, so the solver's individual contribution is not fully isolated.

The VLM comparison is not fully apples-to-apples: the proposed model fine-tunes Qwen3-VL on PARSE-10K, whereas most baselines are evaluated zero-shot. The gains may partly reflect in-domain fine-tuning rather than only the quality of the part-level representation or dataset.

Scene-generation evaluation is primarily qualitative and based on a small user study (20 participants, 12 scenes). Standard quantitative metrics such as FID/KID, scene-graph matching, object-contact accuracy, and physical-stability measures are not reported in the main paper, making the claim of improved realism and contact fidelity less rigorous.

PARSE-10K annotations are generated by the proposed solver and simulation pipeline. Contact labels rely on convex-hull proximity with a 1 mm threshold, and asset part annotations use P3-SAM/GPT with manual canonical-pose verification. The resulting ground truth may contain systematic noise or bias that is not quantified.

The main paper does not clearly report the size or difficulty distribution of the visual relation and part-level contact MCQ test sets, nor does it separate results on the manually labeled COCO real-image subset. The very high MCQ accuracy (97.4%) would be more convincing with clearer controls against question-construction artifacts.

The enforced unique-supporter and DAG structure may not represent all physical configurations, such as objects supported by multiple surfaces or non-tree-like contact/support relations. This limits expressiveness relative to the full space of real indoor arrangements.

strengths: The part-level relational formulation is well motivated and clearly specified. The Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) distinguishes object-level spatial edges from part-level geometric edges, and Table 4 gives a concrete dictionary of relations with their default surfaces and geometric constraints, which makes the representation reproducible in principle.

PARSE-10K is a substantial resource. It contains 10,000 scenes, 17,372 part-segmented assets across 132 categories, averages 49.9 objects per scene, and (per Fig. 13) more than half of the scenes have >50 part-level contacts. Table 1 highlights that it is the only listed dataset that combines layout priors, physical optimization, part annotations, and part-level contact annotations, which is a genuinely useful niche.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is a sensible engineering pipeline: topological ordering of the DAG, coarse-to-fine pruning of the feasible pose space via object-level then part-level constraints, and final validation in SAPIEN. Algorithm 1 and Sec. A.2 give enough detail for a reader to understand the mechanism.

The experimental section has reasonable breadth (three VLM task types plus diffusion-based scene generation), and the Ours(cond) vs. Ours(uncond) user-study comparison does at least isolate the effect of PAG conditioning on generation.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparison is confounded. 'Ours' is Qwen3-VL fine-tuned on data produced by the same pipeline that generated the test set, whereas GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robobrain2.0 and Qwen3-VL are all zero-shot. Without a baseline fine-tuned on a comparable-scale object-level dataset (e.g., 3D-FRONT/3D-SSG-style supervision), the claimed benefit of part-level supervision cannot be separated from dataset size or in-domain adaptation. No such ablation is presented.

All reasoning evaluation is in-domain. The three tasks (visual relation MCQ, part-level contact MCQ, SGG) are constructed from PARSE-10K renders using a predefined relation/part vocabulary, so 97.4%/86.2%/76.6% only demonstrates fitting to the authors' own data distribution. The paper claims to advance 'geometry-grounded spatial reasoning' but evaluates on no external spatial reasoning benchmark.

The generalization claim is not supported by any numbers. The paper states that manually labeled COCO images were added to the test set to verify generalization, but no separate COCO results are reported, and it is never explained how ground-truth part-level contact labels were obtained for real photographs.

Scene-generation evidence is weak and partly contradicts the narrative. It rests entirely on a 20-participant, 3-way forced-choice study (chance = 33%) with no significance testing or inter-annotator agreement, and no standard quantitative metrics (FID/KID, collision rate, physical-stability rate, object/relation counts). InstructScene is trained on a different dataset (3D-FRONT), so the method/data effects are conflated. Notably Ours(uncond) is below chance on Realism (27.5%) and Contact Fidelity (26.3%), undermining the claim that PARSE-10K alone improves realism.

The dataset's central asset - the part-level contact graph - is never validated. Contacts are derived from CoACD convex-hull proximity with a 1 mm threshold, then mapped to the nearest visual-mesh part (Fig. 8, Sec. C.1). No accuracy measurement against human annotation is provided, yet essentially all part-level supervision in the paper depends on the correctness of these labels.

No solver statistics are reported. The paper states that placements failing after MaxTrials are discarded (Sec. A.2), but never gives the failure rate, how failures affect scene completeness, or how many part-level constraints could not be satisfied. This directly affects the claimed physical validity of the 10,000 scenes.

The diversity claim is weakened by the construction protocol: all 10,000 scenes are generated from only 200 hand-designed PAGs across 17 room types (Sec. C.2). Compositional diversity is therefore limited to asset sampling within those templates, and no measure of layout or graph diversity is given.

The asset library is built by mixing PartNeXt/3D-FRONT/ABO/Objaverse with internet images processed by Rodin (generative 3D), P3-SAM (automatic part segmentation) and GPT (part semantic labels), followed by unspecified 'manual verification' (Sec. B). The extent of verification, error rates, and licensing are not discussed, leaving the quality and legality of a core dataset component unverified.

Table 1 appears numerically inconsistent (e.g., HSSD-200 lists 211 scenes and 18,656 objects with 329.7 average objects per scene, which would imply ~88; 3D-FRONT and FumiScene show similar mismatches). The columns or values need correction or clarification.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, e.g. 'substantially improved physical realism', 'significantly advances geometry-grounded spatial reasoning', which are supported only by in-domain evaluations and a small user study.
